reviewRecord.title: Identify the probability controlled by alpha
fairness: Prior-note provenance for this seven-item review: the requested review3fix report did not exist at intake. The seven prior REVISE records were read from docs/research/question-topic-statistics-review3-20261112.json and the candidate packet's round3.fixRound.reviewInput.reviews. Only the seven current round3.proposals[].after candidates are adjudicated; frozen, kept, retired, parked and held records are outside scope. This is an offline editorial review, not fresh source verification or Melissa Rowland's exact-version clinical approval.

Prior category cue addressed: 'Which probability is controlled' replaces 'Which error probability'. All three options now answer the requested category; successful detection cannot be rejected merely because it is not an error.

Type I error probability is the unique best answer in the standard significance-level definition. Beta and true-effect detection probability are credible neighboring misconceptions. 'Controls' appropriately avoids requiring the attained Type I error probability to equal alpha for every test.

The explanation distinguishes rejection of a true null, failure to reject under a specified alternative, and power = 1 - beta. This is high-yield foundational recall; its easy, single-skill construction is appropriate under the owner's statistics exception.

The brief Jordan Ellis employee presentation supplies no answer clue and does not require patient demographics. There is one standalone node, no current update or exhibit, and no later-part dependency. The task is complete when displayed separately; review-only key position is excluded from cue assessment. The same standalone employee frame applies to all seven reviewed items.

reviewRecord.title: Reduce beta through sample size
fairness: In a conventional power calculation for a specified true alternative, increasing sample size with effect, variance and alpha fixed increases power and lowers beta. The task supplies the fixed quantities needed for this basic rule.
The explanation explicitly connects beta to 1 - power and teaches why the keyed direction follows. The three direction choices are parallel. No additional calculation or clinical step is required.

reviewRecord.title: Relate true effect magnitude to power
fairness: For the conventional comparison of effect magnitudes under the tested alternative, larger absolute mean separation with sample size, variance and alpha fixed increases power.

The alternatives are parallel, and the explanation teaches the effect-size/sample-size relationship. This is a clean directional recall question; the fixed inputs prevent confusing a larger true effect with a change in sample size or noise.

reviewRecord.title: Relate the rejection threshold to power
fairness: Lowering alpha shrinks the rejection region of the otherwise fixed z-test and reduces power. Neither an increase nor constancy is the standard result.

The explanation teaches the power/type I error tradeoff. 'Lowering' in the task is needed to identify the changed input and does not itself reveal which direction power takes. One complete recall task.

reviewRecord.title: Relate population variance to power
fairness: For a specified true alternative in the conventional z-test power calculation, greater variance with raw mean difference, sample size and alpha fixed reduces the signal-to-noise ratio and lowers power.

reviewRecord.title: Select a rank test for three independent groups
fairness: Three independent groups with ordinal outcomes identify Kruskal-Wallis among these choices. Mann-Whitney is the two-independent-group competitor; signed-rank concerns paired differences.

The stem appropriately asks about distributions rather than asserting an unrestricted median comparison. Group count and independence are necessary discriminators, not giveaway wording. Feedback teaches the distinction.

reviewRecord.title: Choose the original-scale linear correlation coefficient
fairness: Pearson r is the unique coefficient here for linear association using the original observations. Spearman and Kendall are credible rank-association alternatives.

'Original measurement scales' is reasonably read as original observations rather than ranks; it does not make r a quantity with measurement units. The explanation correctly separates the three coefficients. No extra normality assumption is needed just to calculate or describe r.

reviewRecord.title: Recognize Pearson correlation applied to ranks
fairness: Pearson correlation of the ranked observations defines Spearman rho. Kendall tau instead uses concordance; ordinary Pearson r uses the unranked observations.

Naming Pearson in this definition identifies the operation being transformed and is legitimate content, not a key-only lexical match. The explanation teaches both the rank transformation and the closest alternative. Direct definition recall is acceptable.

reviewRecord.title: Match a continuous conditional mean to regression
fairness: Prior cue addressed: 'when linear-model assumptions hold' is absent from the task and appears only in post-answer feedback. The presentation does not name the keyed model family.

Multiple linear regression is the unique best listed model for mean blood loss conditional on several predictors. Binary logistic regression targets a binary outcome; Cox regression targets event-time hazards. The task asks for model recognition, not whether a particular unseen dataset satisfies model assumptions, so no distribution or diagnostic results are needed to distinguish these options.

The three alternatives are comparably specific regression-model names. 'Several predictors' supplies the multiple-predictor objective but does not alone distinguish these model families; the continuous outcome mean remains the substantive discriminator.

Feedback conditions use of the linear model on its assumptions and contrasts the binary-outcome alternative. Selecting a model by outcome type is a high-yield, easy, single-skill task. The standalone task is complete without an exhibit or previous part.

reviewRecord.title: Compare survival distributions between groups
fairness: Log-rank is the best listed test for a between-group survival-distribution comparison with independent censoring. Mann-Whitney does not generally handle censored event times; a paired t-test also mismatches the independent groups.

The explanation correctly treats proportional hazards as a favorable setting for the test, rather than claiming it is necessary for every valid log-rank null test. The task is complete and the feedback teaches the event/risk-set distinction.

reviewRecord.title: Relate prevalence to NPV
fairness: With the stated sensitivity and specificity held fixed, increasing prevalence lowers NPV. These nondegenerate constructed values make the direction unambiguous.

The model label prevents confusion with measured clinical test performance. Feedback explicitly states the fixed-performance condition and the role of the base rate. No extra arithmetic or clinical step is needed.

reviewRecord.title: Identify the measures with a prevalence term
fairness: PPV/NPV are the unique pair with direct prevalence dependence in the standard formulas. Sensitivity/specificity and likelihood ratios are appropriate same-category competitors.

The qualification 'in the standard diagnostic formulas' avoids claiming that observed sensitivity or specificity can never vary between populations with different disease spectra. The explanation preserves that distinction. No unfair key-only phrase.

fairness: False-positive rate is the unique correct horizontal coordinate of a standard ROC curve. True-positive rate is the vertical-axis misconception; true-negative rate is the failure-to-complement-specificity misconception.
The three labels are parallel. Feedback supplies both axes and the 1 - specificity rule, so a figure is unnecessary for this axis-definition task.

reviewRecord.title: Separate relative reduction from absolute reduction
fairness: Independent calculation: (0.20 - 0.05) / 0.20 = 0.75, or 75%. The 25% alternative is the treatment/control risk ratio, and 15% represents confusing the 15-percentage-point absolute decrease with relative decrease.

The common 30-day horizon, control/treatment identification and constructed-data label are supplied. Feedback shows the formula, substitution and competing quantities. This is one calculation skill, not two consequential reasoning steps.

reviewRecord.title: Identify a reproducible evidence search and appraisal
fairness: The conjunction of a prespecified question, reproducible search, eligibility criteria and appraisal identifies systematic review. Narrative review is the closest credible alternative; a prospective cohort collects participant follow-up rather than synthesizing the literature.

The repeated 'literature' wording occurs in both review choices and does not uniquely reveal the key. The explanation appropriately allows narrative synthesis without requiring meta-analysis. Standalone definition recall is fair.

fairness: Outcome rating that changes solely after learning treatment assignment identifies observer/detection bias. Recall bias and attrition bias involve different stages of information collection or loss.

reviewRecord.title: Recognize results-dependent publication
fairness: Prior cue addressed: the task now describes trials becoming 'available to evidence reviewers' and does not contain 'published' or 'publication'. Recognizing the bias requires connecting results-dependent study availability to the named mechanism.

Publication bias is the unique best answer among these options. Entire trials are selectively unavailable based on their findings; the stem does not describe participant loss within a trial or distorted outcome assessment. Attrition and observer bias are plausible same-category mechanism confusions.
The explanation teaches results-dependent availability and its potential to distort an evidence synthesis, without claiming that every missing study or every small effect proves publication bias.

This is high-yield, easy definition recognition with one skill. The short standalone task specifies the relevant unit and selection mechanism; no patient narrative, exhibit or second decision is needed.

reviewRecord.title: Identify the purpose of random allocation
fairness: Prior cue addressed: 'Ensure recruitment represents the target population' has become 'Improve representation of the target population'. The sampling distractor no longer advertises an absolute guarantee. 'Main inferential purpose' has also been simplified to 'main purpose'.

Balancing prognostic factors in expectation is the unique best answer. Concealing treatment during outcome assessment is blinding, while target-population representation concerns sampling and recruitment rather than random allocation among enrolled participants.

'In expectation' is a necessary accuracy qualification, not a contrast with implausibly absolute competitors in the revised set. The options now have parallel action grammar and comparable scope and length.

Feedback correctly includes measured and unmeasured baseline factors and warns that an individual trial can have chance imbalance. This high-yield allocation-versus-blinding-versus-sampling distinction is suitable as easy, standalone, single-skill recall.

reviewRecord.title: Match blinded assessment to its principal bias target
fairness: Keeping outcome assessors unaware of assignment most directly reduces observer/detection measurement bias. It does not randomize baseline prognostic factors or prevent selective publication.

'Most directly' is appropriate for a bias-prevention question. The three choices name bias targets at comparable specificity. Feedback distinguishes blinding from random allocation; the single-stage mechanism task stands alone.

reviewRecord.title: Recognize an adherence-defined analysis set
fairness: Both prior requested repairs are present: 'protocol criteria' is absent from the task, and feedback now explicitly contrasts as-treated regrouping with the adherence-defined subset.

Per-protocol analysis is the unique best answer for including only participants who sufficiently adhered to their assigned treatment. Intention-to-treat does not make this adherence-based exclusion; as-treated analysis groups by treatment actually received rather than defining the set by adherence to assigned treatment.

'Only' describes the defining subset restriction and is not a gratuitous absolute in a distractor. 'Sufficiently adhered' is adequate for naming the analysis; no invented numerical compliance threshold is required. Feedback appropriately places the criteria in a prespecified framework.

The explanation teaches the selection-bias risk and the closest competing analysis without claiming that per-protocol restriction preserves randomization. All three labels are parallel named analyses. This is high-yield, easy, single-skill recall in a complete standalone task.

reviewRecord.title: Recognize a prespecified acceptable efficacy loss
fairness: The key correctly describes limiting loss relative to control by a prespecified margin. The two-bounds option describes equivalence; the benefit-target option points toward superiority.

A noninferiority result does not prove identical efficacy, and the explanation correctly teaches exclusion of an unacceptable loss through a confidence-interval comparison. This is a direct objective-definition task, so no invented margin, endpoint scale or numerical trial result is needed.

reviewRecord.title: Identify the aim of phase 0 microdosing
fairness: For an exploratory microdose study, early human pharmacokinetic characterization is the best listed objective. Conventional dose tolerability, confirmatory efficacy and postapproval surveillance belong to different development objectives.

The microdose qualifier narrows the scope appropriately; not every exploratory early-phase study has an identical objective. No confident factual error is identified in the explanation, but the registry-classification detail was not independently source-verified in this offline review.

Phase 0 is less central to the conventional board-level phase I-IV sequence; highYield=false is a qualitative prioritization judgment, not verified ABSITE frequency. Lower priority alone does not warrant revision or failure.

reviewRecord.title: Identify the main aim of conventional phase I
fairness: Safety and dose tolerability are the unambiguous best primary objective for a conventional phase I trial. The other options describe phase II activity, confirmatory comparisons and postapproval surveillance.

'Conventional' and 'main objective' appropriately allow contemporary combined-phase designs without requiring them to complicate this basic item. The explanation teaches the phase I/II distinction and does not claim that efficacy can never be examined in phase I.

fairness: Estimating disease-specific therapeutic activity is the best characteristic phase II objective. Continuing safety assessment does not make defining initial safety/dose tolerability equally best as the phase-defining purpose.

reviewRecord.title: Identify the comparative aim of phase III
fairness: Prior fairness concern addressed: the key now reads 'Confirm efficacy in larger comparative trials' rather than requiring comparison with established treatment. Feedback explicitly allows standard treatment or another appropriate control, including placebo when appropriate, and retains ongoing safety monitoring.

Confirmatory comparative efficacy best characterizes phase III among the supplied objectives. Defining initial safety and dose tolerability, estimating preliminary therapeutic activity, and monitoring postapproval safety are credible neighboring phase objectives. Continued safety assessment in phase III does not make initial dose-tolerability characterization equally best for this 'best characterizes' task.

The options use parallel objective verbs and comparable specificity; the modest length difference does not create a meaningful outlier. Neither the task nor presentation rehearses the key. 'Larger' is a qualitative conventional phase distinction, not an invented enrollment threshold.

Feedback distinguishes confirmatory efficacy from preliminary phase II activity and corrects the comparator misconception. Conventional trial-phase objectives are high-yield, easy recall. The one-line standalone task is appropriate under the owner's direction and does not need a second consequential step.

reviewRecord.title: Apply conditional preferences to the feeding prognosis
fairness: Prior clarityIssues[0-1] and suggestion[0] are repaired: this update independently establishes Ruth's inability to decide and Joan's authority, and names Ruth again before reporting her wishes.

Prior cues[0-1] and suggestion[1] are repaired: all options are concrete feeding plans without appended ethical justifications. Neither length nor an evaluative respect-the-patient phrase identifies the key.

Prior fairness[0-2] and suggestion[2]: expected permanent dependence for self-care independently meets the stated refusal condition. The uncertainty about interaction does not negate that separate condition. A defined feeding trial is a credible competing error until the learner applies the whole preference. The removed gaze observation supplies no unsupported consciousness or recovery inference.

Two consequential steps remain: apply the conditional preference to the supplied functional prognosis, then decide whether the uncertainty justifies a feeding trial. This is high-yield substituted judgment, not an independently verified prognosis for a real stroke patient.

Prior fairness[3]: the authority-to-values sequence is coherent; the preceding explanation does not name this feeding plan. This node stands alone with the shared presentation and its own update. The family record-review setting remains explicit.

Prior cue[0], fairness[0] and suggestion[1]: the informed, voluntary, product-specific refusal expressly covers life-threatening hemorrhage. These applicability facts must remain. The agent's contrary request and emergency implied consent cannot displace this instruction in the stated event. Accepted operative bleeding control remains available.

The options are parallel authorization bases rather than rationale-bearing treatment bundles.

reviewRecord.title: Respond to a child's dissent before elective repair
fairness: Prior cues[0-2] and suggestions[0-2]: the preauthorized-return-visit sentence, sedation shortcut and final-legal-refusal extreme are removed. Comfort, reducibility and elective timing preserve the safety basis for deferral. The options compare parental discussion, legal review and joint discussion at the scheduling stage.

Prior fairness[0]: joint review of the child's fear before fixing an operative date is best. Parental permission does not eliminate the child's participation; fear in this ordinary elective consultation does not itself create a legal-authority dispute. The explanation avoids declaring a universal independent legal veto for a 10-year-old.

Prior fairness[1]: supportive discussion remains an easy application of assent and parental permission. The key is no longer selected by an explicitly announced safe next appointment or a coercive sedation foil. No two-step difficulty is claimed or required under the manager allowance.

reviewRecord.title: Emergency treatment despite parental transfusion refusal
fairness: Prior cues[0-2] and suggestions[0-2]: the candidate replaces sentences explicitly refuting nonblood care and court delay with ongoing bleeding and transient response to resuscitation. Surgical control, resuscitation and legal contact are shared context, so the key is no longer the only combined treatment-and-escalation plan.

Prior fairness[0-1]: continued hemorrhage and recurrent weak pulses despite resuscitation establish immediate danger sufficiently to favor emergency protection over awaiting a court or following the parental restriction. This does not require an invented hemoglobin trigger, waiting period or universal legal procedure. Exact local implementation is not independently verified in this offline review.

Prior fairness[2]: the retrospective clinic review is coherent. The phrase about becoming less responsive during an operation does not identify the anesthetic state; I did not use that observation as independent proof of deterioration. Continued bleeding and recurrent circulatory compromise already support the offered emergency pathway.
This is easy, commonly tested child-versus-adult refusal application. It is not a hard two-step resuscitation problem.
suggestions: Optional clarity cleanup: omit the intraoperative responsiveness observation if anesthetic conditions are irrelevant. Do not add an unverified anesthetic state merely to make that observation interpretable; the circulation findings already establish urgency.

The explanation explicitly preserves those limits and does not invent a dose or harm.

reviewRecord.title: Intermittent ileostomy obstruction: investigation before medication escalation
fairness: The best listed answer is contrast-enhanced abdominal CT. The resident must interpret interruption, distension and release as a possible mechanical process despite liquid output, then choose investigation rather than further output suppression. The comfortable interval examination makes the stated assessment stage intelligible.

Loperamide escalation and acid suppression are plausible responses to substantial ileostomy losses but do not resolve the episodic mechanical concern. Bowel ultrasound is a possible investigation, but CT is the stronger general choice for defining a postoperative cause and its extent; the presence of ultrasound does not establish a coequal best answer here.
The wording does not announce obstruction before the choice. Necessary observations, rather than unique option-word repetition, identify the key. Difficulty is moderate, not hard.
Part one stands alone with the presentation and update. Its explanation introduces the reason for imaging but does not teach the local-versus-abdominal stenosis treatment decision in part two.

This is an offline editorial judgment, not fresh verification of guidance or clinical approval. The same limitation applies to all verdicts in this report. Frozen accepted, kept-unchanged, retired, parked and held records were excluded from verdicts; the report covers the eleven offered Round 3 after versions. High-yield labels are qualitative judgments of resident relevance, not verified examination frequencies.
suggestions: In feedback, briefly explain why CT is preferred to the offered ultrasound for this postoperative etiologic assessment; the current explanation discusses only the medication alternatives.

reviewRecord.title: Recurrent superficial stomal stenosis after diminishing dilation benefit
fairness: Local scar excision and rematuration is the best listed answer. The resident must first recognize that recurrent narrowing with progressively shorter relief warrants moving beyond serial dilation, then use the short skin-level lesion, patent abdominal-wall segment and mobile adjacent bowel to choose the extent of reconstruction.

Repeat dilation remains a believable temporizing error after previous benefit; abdominal reconstruction is a believable over-escalation if depth and reach are ignored. The supplied anatomy separates these choices without an invented numerical cutoff.
The short ring and mobile bowel are decision-critical findings, not gratuitous diagnosis labels or wording cues. The three procedure labels have comparable scope and specificity.

The follow-up is coherent and stands alone: it restates the lesion map, dilation response and operative assessment. The earlier CT recommendation does not prohibit a subsequent contrast study, and its explanation does not reveal this treatment key. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the supplied text.

reviewRecord.title: Supplemental PN after symptomatic enteral advancement trials
fairness: Scope: this report reviews only the four revised round3Fix.proposals after candidates at content version question-topic-ostomy-enterocutaneous-fistula.2026-11-12.v3.fix1. The two retired candidates, five frozen round-three PASS items, and other kept, parked and held records receive no new verdict. The paired readiness item was considered only for continuity. All verdicts are offline editorial judgments, not fresh source verification or clinical approval; exact clinical sign-off remains with Melissa Rowland. High-yield and difficulty labels are qualitative resident-relevance judgments, not measured examination frequencies or performance.

Round-three clarity notes are addressed. 'At the current 40 mL/h' and the complete task establish the present rate; 60 mL/h is explicitly a trial. 'Administered energy / assessed need' no longer implies measured absorption. Improved grip strength, slowed but continuing rehydrated weight loss, and symptom resolution at the lower rate provide clinical response evidence beyond the administration percentages.

The prior unresolved advancement-plus-saline comparison is addressed by two symptomatic higher-rate trials with replacement increased in response to measured losses. Vomiting and repeated feed interruptions reduce actual administered energy from 60% to 45% of assessed need despite the higher pump rate. Low urine alone would still not prove that enteral feeding must be abandoned, but the item no longer depends on that inference. It also replaces the former further-advancement option with a concrete current-rate saline plan.

Supplementing current tube feeds with PN is the best listed plan: the resident must recognize a residual nutritional deficit despite a useful lower-rate enteral contribution, then choose supplementation rather than abandoning that contribution or treating the nutrient deficit with saline. Replacing feeds with PN is the credible overreaction to the higher-rate symptoms; symptom resolution and functional improvement at 40 mL/h distinguish it. Increased saline may accompany care but does not meet the demonstrated nutrient deficit and is not a coequal best answer to this nutrition task.

The prior key-only qualifier 'tolerated' is absent from the choices. 'Supplement current tube feeds with parenteral nutrition' and 'Replace current tube feeds with parenteral nutrition' are parallel, similarly specific alternatives; the saline option also retains tube feeding. Thus the key is not uniquely attractive merely for combining two supports. No strong wording overlap, length outlier, convergence, absolute, diagnosis-label or pre-answer teaching shortcut remains.

The numeric observations are constructed patient records, not universal feeding-rate or output thresholds. The explanation remains clinically consistent, although the revised vomiting/interruption trajectory provides stronger justification than its brief emphasis on losses and urine. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the findings support choosing among these plans without claiming to quantify absorption or prove that every possible enteral adjustment has failed.

The named age/sex presentation, short complaint and separated task are clear. This first node stands alone. Its nutrition explanation does not rehearse the later reconstruction-readiness decision; the later record coherently describes recovered appetite, oral food replacing tube feeding, continued PN and subsequent recovery. No new verdict or wording change is proposed for that frozen companion. The two consequential nutrition inferences make this moderate, high-yield application rather than hard subspecialty management.

reviewRecord.title: Fistula reconstruction planning despite persistently low albumin
fairness: Initiating elective reconstruction planning is the best listed step. The resident must weigh actual weight, strength and functional recovery against persistent low albumin, then integrate infection control, prolonged persistence and abdominal recovery when choosing planning over nutritional escalation or continued observation.

Increasing PN is a credible albumin-driven error; continuing observation is a credible persistence/timing error. Neither is made equally appropriate merely by the low laboratory value. The explanation does not claim that nine months is a universal operative deadline.

PASS applies to beginning reconstruction planning, not declaring the patient cleared for immediate surgery. Detailed anatomy and full operative assessment would still be needed before an actual reconstruction; the wording 'Plan' appropriately leaves that work ahead.

The paired chronology is coherent: oral intake replaces tube feeding after appetite returns, while PN continues. The update supplies the current support, recovery and persistence information needed to answer independently. Earlier supplemental-PN feedback does not rehearse this albumin-versus-recovery decision. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

reviewRecord.title: Repair of a fistulizing stenotic ileal anastomosis
fairness: Resection of the old anastomosis with restoration of continuity is the best listed procedure. Contrast reaching distal bowel does not negate significant narrowing when the upstream bowel is markedly dilated; the resident then must select a durable procedure for the scarred segment containing both defects.

Suture plus dilation represents an attempt to preserve bowel while treating the two findings separately. Bypass with continued drainage leaves the diseased fistulizing segment in place. The healthy mobile adjacent bowel, recovered condition and adequate reserve favor resection over these alternatives.

The operative-feasibility findings are necessary to rank procedures rather than decorative permission to perform the key. Options repeat the same anastomotic target and have comparable specificity; no strong nonmedical wording shortcut identified.

This is moderate application of high-yield fistula anatomy and operative management, not a hard subspecialty technique comparison. It stands alone with its presentation and update. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; exact operative suitability still requires clinician sign-off.

reviewRecord.title: Parenteral fluid support after an unsuccessful oral-volume trial
fairness: The prior fluid-composition and sustainable-intake ambiguities are addressed. The exhibit separates sodium-glucose solution from other oral fluid, supplies the solution's measured sodium concentration in the update, and compares a defined original plan with a higher-volume trial. Persistent nausea with larger drinks and inability to sustain further increases provide an observed patient constraint rather than the unsupported conclusion that therapy is optimized.

The prior unresolved oral-escalation competitor is now tested against an actual response: solution intake rises from 1.2 L to 2.0 L, effluent rises from 2.6 L to 3.6 L, urine falls from 0.3 L to 0.2 L, and creatinine rises. These are constructed observations rather than a universal volume cutoff. Alongside the intolerance, they support supplemental parenteral saline after acute repletion over another oral-volume increase. The explanation now explicitly addresses this comparison.

Maintained serial rehydrated weights and strength, with unchanged meals, preserve the previously useful distinction between fluid dependence and macronutrient dependence. They favor saline supplementation over supplemental PN among the offered plans; the item does not require asserting that weight and strength alone constitute a complete nutritional assessment.

Two consequential steps remain: interpret the unsuccessful oral replacement trajectory and then determine the type of parenteral support from the separate nutritional trajectory. An oral solution can have appropriate composition without meeting this patient's fluid needs. Conversely, requiring parenteral fluids does not automatically justify parenteral macronutrients. Both are high-yield errors for residents, supporting moderate difficulty.

No strong nonmedical cue identified. All three options retain 'alongside oral meals' and name a specific support plan of comparable length. 'Larger drinks caused persistent nausea' appropriately constrains the oral competitor but does not distinguish saline from PN; the learner still must interpret the nutritional observations. No diagnosis label, unique task-word match, rhetorical absolute or majority-component convergence selects the key.

The named age/sex, short complaint and maintenance task are clear. Acute repletion is already underway, so the question does not confuse emergency treatment with the subsequent support plan. This is a standalone item. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; PASS does not prescribe a universal saline amount, infusion schedule or fixed oral-volume ceiling. Exact clinical approval remains pending as described in the report scope.

reviewRecord.title: Reversal eligibility changes the operation for a parastomal hernia
fairness: Prioritizing ileostomy reversal with closure of the defect is the best listed strategy. The resident must use the completed disease treatment, assessed anastomotic healing/patency and prior continence to evaluate whether diversion remains necessary, then let that determination change the hernia operation.

Unlike the permanent-stoma item, this option set makes diversion status consequential. Mesh repair with preservation is a credible reflex response to a symptomatic hernia, while relocation unnecessarily retains a temporary diversion when restoration of continuity is supported.

The findings do not merely state 'eligible for reversal.' The diagnosis and protective-stoma history are legitimate starting information for the management task, not inappropriate diagnostic giveaways. Parallel options have no strong nonmedical key cue.

The current reduction and normal passage establish an elective stage. The item stands alone. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in prioritizing reversal; the primary fascial repair wording should not be generalized into a rule against mesh reinforcement for every stoma-closure defect.
suggestions: Keep feedback focused on reversal versus continued diversion. If teaching a particular abdominal-wall closure technique is also intended, that separate comparison needs defect-specific information and clinician review.

reviewRecord.title: Urgent abdominal assessment for below-fascia stoma necrosis
fairness: The prior option-duplication note is addressed. 'Peristomal conduit resection with local rematuration' and 'Superficial debridement with pouching and reassessment' are different extents of treatment, rather than the same local operation repeated with different timing. Together with abdominal exploration, they compare three concrete management responses to the observed depth.

Urgent abdominal exploration with conduit resection is the best listed plan for black nonbleeding mucosa continuing through the fascial ring into the intraperitoneal conduit. The proximal pink bleeding mucosa supplies the viable proximal boundary. Stool passage and normal systemic measurements do not negate the local finding. Neither superficial care nor a purely peristomal reconstruction adequately addresses the described extent. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The depth observation and systemic reassurance from the prior review are preserved. 'Intraperitoneal conduit' legitimately establishes the anatomy needed to choose an abdominal approach; removing it would damage fairness. The key's word 'Urgent' states the actual management timing rather than an unnecessary virtue qualifier. The choices have comparable length and procedural specificity, with no remaining duplicated-local-operation pattern, teaching sentence, rhetorical absolute or unique grammatical fit.

This remains one high-yield safety rule, not two independent consequential steps: extension below the fascia determines the need for urgent abdominal management. The current manager instruction explicitly permits a clean commonly tested safety rule to be easy. It resolves the earlier difficulty-only objection; no artificial additional decision or concealment of the emergency is needed.

The named age/sex, short complaint and complete task are clear. The outside-record frame distinguishes the historical postoperative emergency from the present clinic review. The item stands alone; its explanation follows coherently from the observations and does not claim that normal lactate excludes local ischemia. PASS is editorial and retains the requirement for exact clinical sign-off.

reviewRecord.title: Withholding loperamide during suspected cardiac toxicity
fairness: Both quoted round-three cue phrases are removed: 'above the product-label maximum' is replaced by a neutral documented prescription increase, and 'Which loperamide instruction' is replaced by a medication-plan task. The update supplies symptoms, the before/after QTc observations and metabolic recovery instead of labelling the regimen excessive or announcing toxicity before the answer.

Withholding loperamide is the best listed instruction during the ongoing monitored assessment. Palpitations and syncope with persistent marked QTc prolongation after potassium, magnesium and creatinine return to their usual ranges justify concern for drug toxicity. Halving retains exposure to the suspected agent, while continuing fails to respond to the new symptomatic ECG signal. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the record need not establish proven causation before withholding the suspected drug.

The prior fairness protections are retained: replacement and cardiac monitoring are already underway, the QTc values are patient observations rather than a newly asserted universal treatment threshold, and the explanation says 'suspected' toxicity. Neither the current update nor the explanation implies that a specialist prescription increase by itself warrants withdrawal. No new dose is invented.

All three choices use the same 'current loperamide regimen' object and differ only in the intended medication action. There is no length, specificity, phrase-match or convergence advantage unique to the key. The recent medication increase followed by symptoms remains a strong clinical clue, but it is relevant chronology rather than the former warning-style product-label cue. The ECG trajectory and corrected metabolic abnormalities supply the clinical reason for withdrawal rather than a generic rule to stop any recently increased medicine.

This remains easy safety recognition, not a difficult two-step diagnostic problem. The options focus on withdrawal versus dose reduction versus continuation, so recognition and the safety response are tightly coupled. Under the current manager exception, that is an acceptable high-yield medication-safety objective and is not independently a reason to REVISE. No claim of hard resident-level discrimination is warranted.

The named age/sex presentation, short complaint and complete task are clear. It stands alone, and the outside assessment chronology makes the persistent ECG change after recovery intelligible. The explanation coherently ties withdrawal to the new toxicity signal while fluid support continues. PASS is an offline editorial judgment; clinical approval and fresh source verification are not conferred.

Only the later authorization actually varies across options; this is one consequential rule application, not two independently discriminating steps. Easy is acceptable under the manager's ethics exception. The standalone task is complete.

fairness: Prior notes addressed: the general operative consent now exists in the visible record, and every option states the actual red-cell action and claimed authority. Vague specific-versus-general instruction labels have been removed.

Religious affiliation does not establish preferences for other products; the explanation correctly preserves the patient's accepted measures. The named adult's age, sex, chronology and complete standalone task are present. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

fairness: Prior notes addressed: the actual prohibited arrest procedures are explicit, and a new pulse-present hypotensive event replaces copying an order summary. All choices offer ventilation and vasopressors, so the treatment wording no longer uniquely matches the key.

The patient's applicable documented permission supports treatment while preserving the CPR limits; automatic suspension and fresh surrogate permission are unnecessary. This is an easy authorization-rule application, acceptable under the safety exception.

The subsequent ventilator trial occurs during an explicitly later admission and adds a different agreed endpoint. This explanation does not give that later withdrawal decision. No unsupported resuscitation threshold or new drug regimen is taught.

reviewRecord.title: Apply the agreed ventilator-trial endpoint
fairness: All prior cue repairs are present: failed spontaneous-breathing trials and full dependence replace the team conclusion that the goal is unattainable; the agent asks for application rather than requesting an endorsed withdrawal; the arbitrary additional-organ-failure foil is removed.

The patient defined the endpoint as breathing independently at the agreed reassessment, not proof that eventual recovery is impossible. The findings support ending the trial with anticipatory symptom care. All alternatives now include symptom care, eliminating a uniquely compassionate/comprehensive key.

The later-admission update stands alone and coherently follows the perioperative node. Earlier feedback reinforces honoring preferences but does not supply this endpoint. This remains an easy application of a patient-defined instruction, acceptable under the ethics exception; no universal trial duration is inferred.

reviewRecord.title: Correct misunderstanding of forgoing cosmetic revision
fairness: Prior notes addressed: the presentation no longer announces observation as the answer, and the administrative witness foil is replaced by a substantive benefits discussion. All options name consent content at the same stage.

The patient's own account distinguishes his understanding of operative benefits and harms from his mistaken belief about declining cosmetic treatment. Discussing the course without revision directly addresses that misconception. The alternatives are relevant consent subjects but do not address the stated gap.

This is intentionally an easy single-gap consent question. The clinical indication and patient's account make the rule clear; they do not constitute an extraneous diagnosis label or wording-only key. No second consequential inference is claimed.

reviewRecord.title: Respect the scope of verbal family permission
fairness: The central prior ambiguity is repaired before the choice: the sister requests a spoken conversation, explicitly not copies of records. All choices now answer that request rather than mixing discussion with full-record release.

Limited verbal permission supports dressing-care discussion, not disclosure of the expressly private unrelated diagnosis; a written release is not a prerequisite for the described care conversation. The scope and form alternatives are distinct and the intended key is defensible.

This is an easy permission-boundary application, accepted under the manager exception. The later threat is explicitly a different visit and contains its own exception facts; this feedback does not disclose that later rule. No broader records-release conclusion is implied.

reviewRecord.title: Disclose pertinent facts about a credible imminent threat
fairness: Prior task/category mismatch repaired: every option discloses the same pertinent facts to the same responding police and differs only in whether extra authorization is awaited. The key is no longer the sole disclosure-shaped answer.

Means, identified target, immediate intention, credibility and refusal of permission are supplied. These establish the intended serious-threat exception without implying disclosure of unrelated records. Patient or judicial authorization is not the required prerequisite in the described circumstances.

Necessary threat details appropriately make this easy safety recognition; twoStep=false is not a rejection reason. It stands alone and coherently follows the limited-permission visit. Feedback distinguishes HIPAA permission from state duties, which were not independently verified here.

reviewRecord.title: Respond to payment based on Medicare referrals
fairness: Prior repair is substantive: the draft contract supplies the compensation basis and absence of contracted work, and the stem no longer rehearses the disclosure and education-fund alternatives verbatim.

All choices respond to the same remuneration arrangement. Declining it is the best offered answer; neither disclosure nor changing the destination of payment by itself cures the described referral inducement. No safe-harbor threshold or exception is invented.

The absence of real services is necessary to distinguish the arrangement, although it makes recognition easy. That is permitted for this high-yield professionalism rule. The employee frame appropriately has no fabricated patient demographics; exact legal currency is not newly certified by this offline review.

reviewRecord.title: Arrange emergency evaluation of an acutely impaired surgeon
fairness: Prior safety ambiguity repaired: emergency medical evaluation and ambulance transfer are explicit, while occupational/physician-health processes are placed after immediate care. Sudden speech, gait and identification dysfunction is not labeled intoxication.

Duty relief, the paused case and safe coverage are common context, so the key is no longer the only plan protecting patients or using a specially available replacement. The options now compare assessment routes.

Abrupt neurologic dysfunction warrants emergency assessment; rest or an administrative appointment is not the best initial route. This is deliberately easy urgent-safety recognition, not two-step diagnostic reasoning. Preserving warning signs is necessary and appropriate.

reviewRecord.title: Use a process for a disputed intervention
fairness: The persistent nonurgent dispute after repeated discussions supports institutional ethics/dispute-resolution review, rather than treating authorization as an obligation to operate or proceeding immediately to court.

The learner must recognize that authorization does not establish achievable benefit, then choose the appropriate next process while support continues. This is a high-yield conflict-resolution application.

The outside-chart review and present decision are understandable without another node. The explanation identifies ethics review and applicable appeal procedures rather than asserting a universal unilateral-withdrawal rule.
Jurisdiction-specific appeal obligations have not been verified offline; no confident contradictory clinical claim is identified.

reviewRecord.title: Separate treatment goals from recipient benefit
fairness: Prior clarity and role-label concerns addressed: the task asks the purpose of a treatment-goals discussion and every option supplies that purpose. Overlapping procurement/recovery counselor labels and premature declaration of an established DCD plan are gone.

The agent's uncertainty supplies the actual conflict. Whether ventilation serves the patient's values and goals should govern the discussion; recipient benefit and donation authorization do not substitute for that assessment. This is a clean easy ethical rule, not two-step reasoning.

The explanation narrows the earlier categorical counseling statement by distinguishing referral and responses to agent-initiated questions from OPO-initiated donation discussion. This addresses the prior policy-boundary concern in the wording; the exact current OPTN requirement was not freshly verified offline. The next node concerns death declaration and its specific exclusion is not taught here.

reviewRecord.title: Assign an eligible death-declaring physician
fairness: Prior task and credential concerns addressed: the task asks only who may declare death; each physician meets the supplied local credential requirement, and current assignments are explicit with no hidden additional roles. No combined palliation role or universal declaration interval is asserted.

The bedside-care physician is the uniquely defensible offered choice under the stated separation requirement; both recovery and transplantation of this donor's organs are covered. Numeric option labels are parallel and require reading the assignments.

Earlier feedback now concerns treatment goals rather than teaching the death-declaration exclusions. It still reinforces general independence, so the sequence remains easy rule application, acceptable under the manager exception. Later authorization is explicit and the node stands alone. Actual current OPTN policy was not independently reverified offline.

reviewRecord.title: Use the depth of stoma injury
fairness: The reported nonviability continuing through the fascial opening supports urgent operative revision rather than delayed local care, despite a soft abdomen and effluent passage.

Two steps are supported: interpret the depth of injury, then decide urgency and extent of management despite falsely reassuring function. Superficial versus deep necrosis is a high-yield surgical distinction.
An endoscopic viability finding is legitimate data for this management task, not a diagnosis-label giveaway. The named patient's retrospective assessment is clear and self-contained.
No confident clinical inaccuracy or nonmedical wording shortcut identified.

reviewRecord.title: Investigate intermittent obstructive symptoms with watery output
fairness: Both prior clarity defects are repaired: current resolution, drinking, effluent passage and a soft nondistended abdomen distinguish this clinic evaluation from active unresolved obstruction; every choice names a concrete imaging investigation.

The key no longer embeds the diagnosis or competes with unnamed treatment escalations. The resident must infer possible intermittent obstruction from stop-start output, cramps, distension and decompression, then select CT as the best offered investigation for the abdominal cause.

The later fluid-replacement decision is distinct, and this unchanged explanation does not provide its answer. CT is not claimed to exclude every intermittent event when normal, and no contrast protocol, invented timing or dosing rule is required to distinguish these offered modalities. The precise contemporary imaging guideline was not newly verified offline; no confident clinical error identified.

fairness: The described rise in ileostomy losses and fall in urine after increasing plain water support emphasizing an appropriate sodium-glucose replacement rather than more hypotonic water or a low-sodium sports drink.
The learner interprets the fluid-loss response and applies small-bowel replacement physiology. Sodium composition is decision-relevant, not an unfair wording cue.

The update supplies the hospital reassessment and outpatient context locally, so it stands alone. In sequence it moves from evaluation of intermittent obstruction to replacement after reassessment without earlier answer leakage.

The explanation appropriately retains monitoring and possible parenteral rehydration if depletion recurs; the item must not be interpreted as declaring falling urine harmless. No exact recipe or threshold is invented.

reviewRecord.title: Use defined distal anatomy for nutrition
fairness: Accessible patent distal bowel plus controlled sepsis makes a supervised distal-feeding trial a reasonable next consideration, particularly with recurrent central-line complications. Increasing proximal oral intake repeats the documented loss problem.

Two consequential steps connect anatomic feasibility with the balance between enteral use and ongoing parenteral complications. The cautious 'consider' task and supervised trial do not promise immediate nutritional independence.

Information on distal access, patency and adequate bowel is necessary eligibility information rather than an optional answer hint. Parenteral support remains a credible competitor when distal feeding is inadequate.
This is relevant advanced fistula-nutrition content for surgery boards. No confident clinical error identified; exact suitability remains for clinician review.

reviewRecord.title: Plan reconstruction for a persistent fistula with distal obstruction
fairness: Prior unsupported specificity is removed: the key calls for operative reconstruction planning with specialists, not a particular staged operation or technique. The explanation explicitly avoids a universal waiting interval.
The prior fix-versus-retain-the-stenosis cue is gone. All options are concrete specialist management strategies with parallel scope; the wrong labels no longer advertise an unresolved defect.

Fixed downstream obstruction changes the expectation of closure and the appropriateness of tract-directed closure, while recovered nutrition, strength and fluid balance after source control support reconstruction planning rather than indefinite support. Those are two meaningful high-yield inferences. The question does not assert readiness for immediate surgery or specify an unsupported operative date.

fairness: Repeated failure of appliance care plus intermittent obstructive symptoms supports surgical assessment, while present reducibility, normal output and absence of acute symptoms support elective rather than emergency assessment.

The learner must decide both whether conservative management has been adequate and how urgently to escalate. All choices are referral/assessment plans, and the urgency distinction has clinical consequences.
The prior attempted refitting is meaningful treatment-response evidence, not merely a named missing step. The current findings are needed to distinguish elective from urgent escalation.
The item is self-contained and high-yield. It appropriately avoids unsupported ranking of mesh or operative technique.

fairness: Prior notes addressed: this is now an employee simulation frame; all options introduce a proposed identifier comparison rather than repeating an explicitly failed screen check. The wristband and requisition provenance is supplied instead of assuming either is independent.

The resident must recognize that three matching printed artifacts can inherit the same wrong-record selection, then choose the actor-provided identifiers to challenge that failure. Wristband-versus-label checking is ordinarily plausible; its inferiority here depends on the stated shared generation process.

The spoken-versus-printed distinction is causally relevant to the supplied process, not merely a uniquely elaborate label. The feedback appropriately describes a control to pilot and evaluate, not demonstrated effectiveness or a complete universal identification protocol. The standalone task is complete.

reviewRecord.title: Verify the operation with the current operating team
fairness: Prior hidden-participant problem repaired: the block check's participants, the later team additions and each proposed verification plan are explicit before the choice. The rationale no longer invents a two-person limitation absent from the option.

All options address identity, procedure and site before incision. The meaningful difference is current joint participation versus a check while anesthesia is occupied or a briefing about the earlier block-room event. The operating-team verification is the best offered plan.

The earlier invasive step and personnel transition provide a real setting for the rule, although applying it remains easy. This is acceptable safety recognition; no unsupported additional negative, second-step claim or universal staffing roster is needed.

reviewRecord.title: Choose a response based on behavior
fairness: The intentional normalized shortcut with unrecognized risk supports coaching and correction of incentives, rather than treating it as an inadvertent slip or established reckless disregard.
Two meaningful steps are present: classify the behavior from intent/risk perception, then select a response without allowing different patient outcomes to change that classification.
All three choices share the system repair, so the key is not uniquely comprehensive. The deliberate action makes consolation a credible near-miss, while harm makes punitive action tempting.
This is a high-yield just-culture application. It is clear and self-contained; no confident clinical or fairness error identified.

reviewRecord.title: Stop unnecessary prophylaxis despite a remaining drain
fairness: Prior notes addressed: simple mastectomy without reconstruction supplies the operation; normal temperature, serous drainage and apposed nonerythematous wound edges replace the interpretive sentence declaring no treatment indication. The stem no longer announces the drain as the team's reason for antibiotics.

The vague 'through wound review' alternative is replaced by the clear future endpoint of complete incisional healing. All options compare prophylaxis plans, with stop-now the best offered answer for this closed clean incision without supplied evidence requiring treatment.

The task explicitly concerns prophylaxis, so this remains chiefly a single stewardship-rule application rather than two consequential steps. Easy is permissible here. No reconstruction-specific regimen, antibiotic dose or invented numeric duration is asserted; normal findings are not claimed to exclude every possible infection.

reviewRecord.title: Choose risk adjustment for hospital benchmarking
fairness: Both prior substantive corrections are present: the task specifies fair hospital-quality benchmarking, and the explanation explicitly says equal median ages do not establish equal age distributions. The option feedback no longer claims matched age distributions or individual matching.

Same procedure category and complete 30-day follow-up do not resolve the displayed urgency and functional-dependence differences. Multivariable adjustment is the best offered approach; age stratification or a procedure-specific crude comparison leaves relevant measured differences unaddressed. Adjustment does not establish a causal quality difference.

This follows the owner statistics exception: one skill, a labeled constructed exhibit, parallel methods options and concise feedback. Counting whitespace-separated words with the displayed name gives 17 prose words plus 23 exhibit words, 40 combined before the task. Easy and twoStep=false are appropriate.

reviewRecord.title: Thigh biopsy method and approach
fairness: Independent round-2 review dated 2026-11-12. Summary: 2 PASS, 1 REVISE, 0 FAIL. Reviewed the current JSON packet, companion Markdown, prior independent review and recorded source ledger. Read the round-2 definition/module and archived round-1 packet to check the actual revised content rather than accepting author responses. The before projections match the archived round-1 after fields; the current update, task, exhibit, explanation and option labels match the round-2 definitions for all three items. All eleven claims and twelve source records equal their archived versions. The prior review hash matches the packet. All 36 prior fairness/suggestion notes are accounted for below. No Git, network, installs or agents used. Citations refer to the packet's recorded evidence, not fresh inspection of external publications. PASS is an editorial judgment on the draft, not clinical approval: all three remain needs_clinician_review pending Melissa Rowland's explicit version-specific sign-off and confirmation of the constructed access and operative geometry.

Reviewed version: question.soft-tissue-mass.specialist-planned-biopsy.v1.r6. Confusion FIXED: anterior skin through rectus femoris and medial skin through adductor longus then rectus femoris are concrete routes. The two-column table directly connects each route to enhancement and relative length. No abstract path, region, target or corridor letter labels occur in the after fields, revised rationales or explanation. Historical before/originalLive fields appropriately retain the original wording.

Prior fairness notes 1-3 and suggestions 1 and 3: addressed at draft level. The update explicitly restores percutaneous access to both enhancing solid targets. Adductor longus replaces generic adductor muscle in the table, both medial choices and relevant feedback. The initial anterior image-guided core key and method-by-route decision are preserved. The packet's claim.qq20261102b.sarcoma-initial-core-method supports feasible initial core sampling, with open biopsy a selected alternative: Serrano et al., SEOM-GEIS guideline, Clin Transl Oncol. 2025;27:1460-1471, doi:10.1007/s12094-024-03842-5 (source.qq20261102b.seom2024), and Noebauer-Huhmann et al., ESSR technique guidance, Semin Musculoskelet Radiol. 2015;19:475-482, doi:10.1055/s-0035-1569251 (source.qq20261102b.essr2015). No competing best answer identified on the stated case observations.

Prior fairness note 4 and suggestion 2: the missing resection relationship is supplied. The proposed longitudinal anterior resection includes the anterior skin entry and underlying rectus femoris, while adductor longus lies outside the specimen. Combined with the displayed route, this establishes the intended tract-to-resection relationship at vignette level. The rationale and explanation explicitly require removal of the tract including its entry with the definitive specimen and distinguish that from same-compartment access. This maps to claim.question-topic-soft-tissue-sarcoma-desmoid.tract-excision: Hayes et al., UK guidelines, Br J Cancer. 2025;132:11-31, published online 2024, doi:10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y (source.question-topic-soft-tissue-sarcoma-desmoid.uk-2024), and SEOM-GEIS, doi:10.1007/s12094-024-03842-5 (source.question-topic-soft-tissue-sarcoma-desmoid.seom-geis-2024). The prior request for clinician confirmation itself remains pending; invented case observations and general guidance do not constitute that confirmation. This is an explicit clinical acceptance boundary, not a remaining omission of the planning information from the draft.

Prior fairness notes 5-6: addressed. Both targets remain enhancing solid intramass tissue; the stronger enhancement does not require taking the route through additional uninvolved tissue. Claim.qq20261102a.sarcoma-viable-biopsy-target is retained and mapped to enhancement and explanation, with direct support recorded from ESSR 2015, doi:10.1055/s-0035-1569251 (source.qq20261102a.essr2015-target); the newer SEOM source corroborates the general pathway rather than independently verifying the exact targeting rule. Claim.qq20261102b.sarcoma-method-and-tract supports avoiding a separate unaffected compartment. Exact muscle membership is supported in the packet by claim.qq20261102b.rectus-anterior-compartment, Szczerba et al., J Clin Med. 2026;15:5547, doi:10.3390/jcm15145547, and claim.qq20261102b.adductor-medial-compartment, Santamaria-Le Pera et al., Surg Radiol Anat. 2025;47:74, doi:10.1007/s00276-025-03567-2. These records do not certify the constructed needle trajectory. Duplicate ESSR and SEOM records are not independent sources.

Prior fairness note 7 and suggestion 4, fairness component: retained. The four options each have 10 whitespace-delimited words excluding the review-only key marker, use parallel grammar and cross both methods with both routes. Neither length, specificity nor an odd-one-out qualifier reveals the key. The specimen observation appropriately narrows the route but leaves two options; core-method knowledge is still required. The shorter medial route and stronger enhancement remain competing observations. Key-first display is explicitly review-only. Runtime shuffling and wait display were not exercised in this offline content review.

Prior fairness note 8: moderate at the easier end. The learner combines initial biopsy-method selection with a removable tract and competing enhancement/length information. Explicit specimen boundaries reduce the anatomical inference compared with round 1; this is not a hard item. Difficulty is a qualitative judgment, not measured performance.

Prior fairness note 9 and suggestion 4, style/status components: addressed. The packet now displays Enlarging limb mass (3 words). The presentation uses the runtime patient-name token, age 39 and female sex, and a concrete clinic visit. The task now completely asks for an initial tissue-sampling plan for the named patient's thigh mass. No abstract 'A patient with' opening or complaint/presentation duplication. Actual name substitution was not rendered. Concept identity and needs_clinician_review status remain explicit. No claim that all prior requests are clinically closed is warranted while specialist confirmation remains outstanding.
suggestions: No blocking wording revision. Preserve the balanced choices, exact adductor-longus terminology, site-specific task and evidence limitations.

Before clinical acceptance, obtain Melissa Rowland's version-specific confirmation of feasible access and the entire entry-to-target tract within the proposed specimen; do not treat this PASS or the original flag as approval.

reviewRecord.title: Upper-arm biopsy method and approach
fairness: Reviewed version: question.soft-tissue-mass.specialist-planned-biopsy.v2.r6, replacing the owner's flagged v2.r4 through the round-1 v2.r5 draft. D97-1's offline scope and clinical-approval limitations apply. Prior fairness note 1: confusion FIXED. Posterior skin through triceps and anterior skin through biceps then triceps replace the abstract letter mappings, with target enhancement and route length aligned in the table. Revised choices and feedback contain no path/region letters.

Prior fairness notes 2-3 and suggestion 1: addressed. Both enhancing targets now explicitly permit percutaneous sampling. The same posterior image-guided core plan remains the best offered initial method and route. Claim.qq20261102b.sarcoma-initial-core-method supports the initial feasible core method, and claim.qq20261102b.sarcoma-method-and-tract supports avoiding another unaffected compartment: Noebauer-Huhmann et al., ESSR 2015, doi:10.1055/s-0035-1569251 (source.qq20261102b.essr2015), and Serrano et al., SEOM-GEIS 2024 guideline, published 2025, doi:10.1007/s12094-024-03842-5 (source.qq20261102b.seom2024). Open incisional biopsy remains a selected alternative rather than universally wrong. The arm-membership claims claim.qq20261102b.biceps-anterior-compartment and claim.qq20261102b.triceps-posterior-compartment cite Lombardi et al., Magnetic resonance imaging of the elbow, Pol J Radiol. 2020;85:e440-e460, doi:10.5114/pjr.2020.98691 (source.qq20261102b.arm-anatomy). This single recorded anatomy source supports membership, not the complete trajectory's safety.

Prior fairness note 4 and suggestion 2: the draft-level omission is repaired. The longitudinal posterior resection includes the posterior entry and underlying triceps; biceps is outside the proposed specimen. The displayed posterior route therefore follows the stated exposure, and the rationale/explanation explicitly require subsequent removal of the entry and tract with the specimen. Avoiding biceps alone is expressly distinguished from proving resectability. Claim.question-topic-soft-tissue-sarcoma-desmoid.tract-excision maps this rule to Hayes et al., UK guidelines, Br J Cancer. 2025;132:11-31, doi:10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y (source.question-topic-soft-tissue-sarcoma-desmoid.uk-2024), and SEOM-GEIS, doi:10.1007/s12094-024-03842-5 (source.question-topic-soft-tissue-sarcoma-desmoid.seom-geis-2024). The prior request for clinician-confirmed geometry is not completed: the packet explicitly says no clinician confirmation has occurred. That remains a clinical sign-off requirement despite the editorial PASS.

Prior fairness note 5: retained and correctly mapped. Both solid intramass targets enhance. Greater enhancement along the anterior route does not override tract planning. Claim.qq20261102a.sarcoma-viable-biopsy-target cites ESSR 2015, doi:10.1055/s-0035-1569251 (source.qq20261102a.essr2015-target), with SEOM corroboration of the general core pathway. The older direct-technique limitation remains; duplicate publications do not supply independent corroboration. Enhancement does not establish histology.

Prior fairness note 6 and suggestion 3, option component: retained. All four choices have 9 whitespace-delimited words excluding the review key marker. Both methods occur with both routes, with equal specificity and no key-only qualifier. The stated posterior specimen relationship eliminates two routes but does not identify the method by word matching. No knowledge-free unique key cue identified. The shorter anterior route and stronger enhancement remain plausible attractions. Runtime randomization is declared, not independently exercised here.

Prior fairness note 7: moderate at the easier end. Two familiar decisions remain, although explicitly stating the resection field makes route selection easier than round 1. Readability is improved without a new ambiguous anatomical puzzle.

Prior fairness note 8 and suggestion 3, style/status components: addressed. Enlarging limb mass is 3 words; the presentation uses a patient-name token, age 52 and female sex. The complete task now names the upper-arm mass. Authored patient style is satisfied; actual runtime name rendering was not tested. Stable concept/key and needs_clinician_review status are retained.

Nonblocking packet-copy error found independently: selfCheck.sourceClosure refers to adductor longus, and evidenceMapping[0].type refers to the thigh medial muscle; the ledger repeats the latter text. Those statements belong to D97-1. Actual arm claim IDs and the player-facing arm content are correct, so this does not change the question verdict, but the author response is not an entirely clean provenance record.
suggestions: No blocking player-facing revision. Correct the copied thigh/adductor wording in D97-2 selfCheck.sourceClosure and evidenceMapping[0].type, including the corresponding ledger mapping, to describe the retained arm observations and biceps/triceps claims.
Keep clinical acceptance pending Melissa Rowland's explicit version-specific review of feasible access, skin entry and complete posterior tract/specimen geometry.
